item.prompt: According to the passage, why did the signs on the main street grow so large?
item.passage:
Three hundred years ago, the main street of Hallowmere looked very different from today. Above almost every shop door hung a painted wooden sign with a picture on it. A baker showed a loaf of bread, a shoemaker showed a boot, and a locksmith showed a large golden key. These pictures rarely changed, and a shop often kept the same sign for a hundred years, even after a new family took it over.

The pictures had a practical purpose. Many people in the town could not read, so a written name over the door would have helped only a few customers. A picture could be understood by everyone, including farmers who came in from nearby villages on market day.

The signs also worked as addresses. Houses had no numbers yet, so people gave directions by naming the pictures. A letter might be sent to the tailor beside the green hen, and the messenger would know exactly where to go.

Over time, however, the signs became a problem. Shopkeepers competed to hang the biggest ones, and some stretched halfway across the street. They blocked light from upper windows and creaked loudly in the wind. In 1771, after a heavy sign fell and injured a horse, the town council ordered that every sign be fixed flat against the wall. Later, when the town began to number its houses, many shops replaced their pictures with painted names.
choices: Painters charged the same amount for a sign of any size.
Visitors from the villages found small signs hard to see.
Shop owners were trying to do better than one another.
The town council asked shops to make their signs bigger.
item.correct_answer: Shop owners were trying to do better than one another.
item.explanation: "Shop owners were trying to do better than one another." is correct: the passage says "Shopkeepers competed to hang the biggest ones", so each owner was trying to beat the others.

distractor_rationales.choice: Visitors from the villages found small signs hard to see.
distractor_rationales.reason: "Visitors from the villages found small signs hard to see." is wrong because the passage gives a different reason for the size: "Shopkeepers competed to hang the biggest ones"; the villagers are mentioned only as people who could understand pictures.

distractor_rationales.choice: The town council asked shops to make their signs bigger.
distractor_rationales.reason: "The town council asked shops to make their signs bigger." is wrong because the council acted against the signs: it "ordered that every sign be fixed flat against the wall"; the size came from the fact that "Shopkeepers competed to hang the biggest ones".

distractor_rationales.choice: Painters charged the same amount for a sign of any size.
distractor_rationales.reason: "Painters charged the same amount for a sign of any size." is wrong because the passage explains the size in another way: "Shopkeepers competed to hang the biggest ones".

itep.title: The picture signs of Hallowmere
itep.why: Shopkeepers competed to hang the biggest ones

item.prompt: What is the passage mainly about?
item.passage:
Have you ever noticed that a bowl of fruit often seems to ripen all at once? There is a simple reason for this. As many fruits ripen, they give off a gas called ethylene. The gas is invisible, but it works like a signal. When nearby fruit takes in the gas, it begins to ripen as well, and then it releases more ethylene of its own.

Ripening brings several changes. The fruit becomes softer, and its color often changes from green to yellow or red. In bananas and many other fruits, starch turns into sugar, so the fruit tastes sweeter. Bananas, tomatoes and avocados keep ripening after they are picked. Other fruits, such as grapes, strawberries and oranges, do not ripen much more once they leave the plant.

Farmers and shops make use of these facts. Bananas are usually picked while they are still green and hard, because firm fruit travels well on long journeys. Near the end of the trip, they are often kept in warm rooms with a little added ethylene, which helps them ripen evenly before they reach the shops.

You can use the same idea at home. To ripen a hard avocado faster, put it in a paper bag with a ripe banana. The bag holds the gas close to the avocado. To slow ripening down, keep ripe fruit away from other fruit, or store it somewhere cool.
choices: a quick way to soften a hard avocado in a paper bag at home
how the gas ethylene protects fruit from ripening too early
how a ripening gas from fruit works and how people use it
the natural changes that happen to fruit after it forms
item.correct_answer: how a ripening gas from fruit works and how people use it
item.explanation: "how a ripening gas from fruit works and how people use it" is correct: paragraph 1 explains that ripening fruit gives off "a gas called ethylene" that makes nearby fruit ripen, and paragraphs 3 and 4 show that "Farmers and shops make use of these facts" and "You can use the same idea at home".

distractor_rationales.choice: how the gas ethylene protects fruit from ripening too early
distractor_rationales.reason: "how the gas ethylene protects fruit from ripening too early" is wrong about what the gas does: "When nearby fruit takes in the gas, it begins to ripen as well".

distractor_rationales.choice: a quick way to soften a hard avocado in a paper bag at home
distractor_rationales.reason: "a quick way to soften a hard avocado in a paper bag at home" is only the last paragraph ("To ripen a hard avocado faster, put it in a paper bag"); the passage also covers the gas, the changes and how "Farmers and shops make use of these facts".

distractor_rationales.choice: the natural changes that happen to fruit after it forms
distractor_rationales.reason: "the natural changes that happen to fruit after it forms" is too general: the passage is about one cause of ripening, "a gas called ethylene", and how people use it, not every change in fruit.

itep.title: The ripening gas
itep.why: As many fruits ripen, they give off a gas called ethylene.

Farmers and shops make use of these facts. Bananas are usually picked while they are still green and hard, because firm fruit travels well on long journeys. Near the end of the trip, they are often kept in warm rooms with a little added ethylene, which helps them ripen evenly before they reach the shops.

You can use the same idea at home. To ripen a hard avocado faster, put it in a paper bag with a ripe banana. The bag holds the gas close to the avocado. To slow ripening down, keep ripe fruit away from other fruit, or store it somewhere cool.
choices: Bananas are picked after they have turned yellow on the plant.
Bananas are given ethylene as soon as they are picked.
Bananas are kept in cold rooms near the end of their trip.
Bananas are less sweet when picked than when they reach the shops.
item.correct_answer: Bananas are less sweet when picked than when they reach the shops.
item.explanation: "Bananas are less sweet when picked than when they reach the shops." is correct: bananas "are usually picked while they are still green and hard" and ripen "before they reach the shops", and "In bananas and many other fruits, starch turns into sugar, so the fruit tastes sweeter".

distractor_rationales.reason: "Bananas are picked after they have turned yellow on the plant." is wrong: "Bananas are usually picked while they are still green and hard".

distractor_rationales.choice: Bananas are given ethylene as soon as they are picked.
distractor_rationales.reason: "Bananas are given ethylene as soon as they are picked." is wrong: the ethylene comes later: "Near the end of the trip, they are often kept in warm rooms with a little added ethylene".

distractor_rationales.choice: Bananas are kept in cold rooms near the end of their trip.
distractor_rationales.reason: "Bananas are kept in cold rooms near the end of their trip." is wrong: "Near the end of the trip, they are often kept in warm rooms".
